{{Short description|Eigenvalue transformation method}}

{{distinguish| text=the [[Schwinger variational principle]] or  [[Schwinger's quantum action principle]]}}

In  [[mathematics]] the '''Birman–Schwinger principle''' is a useful technique to reduce the eigenvalue problem for an unbounded [[differential operator]] (such as a [[Schrödinger operator]]) to an eigenvalue problem for a bounded integral operator. It originates from independent work by [[Mikhail Shlyomovich Birman|M. Sh. Birman]]<ref name="B1961">"{{cite journal | last1 = Birman | first1 = M. Sh. | title = On the spectrum of singular boundary-value problems | journal = Matematicheskii Sbornik |series=New Series | volume = 55 | pages = 125–174 | year = 1961 | issue = 97 | language = Russian | url=https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=sm&paperid=4754&option_lang=eng}} English translation: Amer. Math. Soc. Transl., Ser. 2, vol. 53, pp. 23–80, 1966.</ref> and [[Julian Schwinger|J. Schwinger]]<ref name=SCH1961>{{cite journal | last1 = Schwinger | first1 = J. | title = On the bound states of a given potential | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 47 | pages = 122–129 | year = 1961| issue = 1 | doi= 10.1073/pnas.47.1.122 | pmid = 16590804 | pmc = 285255 | bibcode = 1961PNAS...47..122S | doi-access = free }}</ref> in 1961.

The Birman–Schwinger principle has found numerous applications in deriving bounds on the discrete eigenvalues of differential operators. One of its most prominent uses is in the original proof of the [[Lieb–Thirring inequality]].

== Statement of the principle for self-adjoint Schrödinger operators ==

The technique was developed for [[self-adjoint]] Schrödinger operators <math>-\Delta - V</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> with real-valued potentials <math>V:\mathbb{R}^n \to [0,\infty)</math>. If <math>\lambda < 0</math> is a negative [[eigenvalue]] of the Schrödinger operator with corresponding [[eigenfunction]] <math>\psi \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>, then the eigenequation

<math>
-\Delta \psi - V \psi = \lambda \psi
</math>

can be formally rearranged to

<math>
\sqrt{V}(-\Delta - \lambda)^{-1} \sqrt{V} \, \phi = \phi
</math>

with <math>\phi = \sqrt{V} \psi</math>. This equation shows that <math>\phi</math> is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue 1 of the Birman–Schwinger operator

<math>
K_\lambda = \sqrt{V}(-\Delta - \lambda)^{-1} \sqrt{V}.
</math>

The Birman–Schwinger principle rigorously formalises this idea, establishing that <math>\lambda < 0</math> is an eigenvalue of the Schrödinger operator [[if and only if]] 1 is an eigenvalue of <math>K_\lambda</math> of the same multiplicity. Additionally, the principle asserts that the number <math>N_\lambda</math> of eigenvalues of the Schrödinger operator less than or equal to <math>\lambda < 0</math> coincides with the number of eigenvalues of <math>K_\lambda</math> greater than or equal to 1, i.e.,

<math>
N_\lambda = \# \{ \text{eigenvalues of } K_\lambda \text{ greater than or equal to } 1 \}.
</math>

The statement requires regularity assumptions on the potential <math>V</math> which ensure that <math>K_\lambda</math> is bounded and compact.<ref name="FLW2022">{{cite book | last1 = Frank | first1 = R. L. | last2 = Laptev | first2 = A. | last3 = Weidl | first3 = T. | title = Schrödinger Operators: Eigenvalues and Lieb–Thirring Inequalities | publisher = Cambridge University Press | year = 2022 | location = Cambridge | series = Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics | volume = 200 | isbn = 978-1-009-21843-6 | doi=10.1017/9781009218436}}</ref>

The usefulness of this spectral equivalence lies in the fact that the integral kernel of <math>K_\lambda</math> is well known. By the Birman–Schwinger principle, upper bounds on <math>N_\lambda</math> can be obtained by considering [[Schatten norm|Schatten norms]] of <math>K_\lambda</math>.

== The Birman–Schwinger bound ==

The [[integral kernel]] of <math>K_\lambda</math> takes the form

<math>
K_\lambda(x,y) = \sqrt{V(x)} G_\lambda(x - y) \sqrt{V(y)}
</math>

where <math>G_\lambda(x - y)</math> is the integral kernel of the free [[Resolvent_formalism|resolvent]] <math>(-\Delta - \lambda)^{-1}</math>. In dimension <math>n = 3</math>, it is explicitly given by

<math>
K_\lambda(x,y) = \sqrt{V(x)} \frac{e^{-\sqrt{-\lambda} |x - y|}}{4\pi |x - y|} \sqrt{V(y)}.
</math>

Computing the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of <math>K_\lambda</math>, Birman<ref name ="B1961"/> and Schwinger<ref name = "SCH1961"/> independently proved the bound

<math>
N_0 \leq \frac{1}{(4\pi)^2} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \frac{V(x)V(y)}{|x - y|} \, dx \, dy.
</math>

By the [[Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality]], the term on the right is further bounded by

<math>
\frac{1}{4(4\pi)^{2/3}} \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} V(x)^{3/2} \, dx \right)^{4/3}.
</math>

In contrast, [[Lieb–Thirring inequality#Lieb–Thirring constants|Weyl asymptotics]] for large coupling involve only the term <math>\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} V(x)^{3/2} \, dx</math>, without the power <math>4/3</math>. An upper bound of this form on <math>N_0</math> can also be derived using the Birman–Schwinger principle. The result corresponds to an endpoint case of the [[Lieb–Thirring inequality]], commonly referred to as the Cwikel–Lieb–Rozenblum bound.

== Extensions of the principle ==

In some applications, it is advantageous to define the Birman–Schwinger operator as

<math>
K_\lambda = (-\Delta - \lambda)^{-1/2} V (-\Delta - \lambda)^{-1/2}
</math>

instead. In particular, in one dimension <math>n = 1</math>, this approach allows for [[Distribution_(mathematics)|distributional]] potentials.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hundertmark | first1 = D. | last2 = Lieb | first2 = E. H. | last3 = Thomas | first3 = L. E. | title = A sharp bound for an eigenvalue moment of the one-dimensional Schrödinger operator | journal = Advances in Theoretical and Mathematical Physics | volume = 2 | issue = 4 | pages = 719–731 | year = 1998 | arxiv=math-ph/9806012| doi= 10.4310/ATMP.1998.v2.n4.a2}}</ref>

While originally established for self-adjoint Schrödinger operators, it is possible to extend the principle to the non self-adjoint case. For <math>\lambda \in \mathbb{C} \setminus [0,\infty)</math>, the Birman–Schwinger operator can then be defined as

<math>
K_\lambda = \operatorname{sgn}(V) \sqrt{|V|}(-\Delta - \lambda)^{-1} \sqrt{|V|}.
</math>

Again, <math>\lambda</math> is an eigenvalue of the Schrödinger operator <math>-\Delta - V</math> if and only if 1 is an eigenvalue of <math>K_\lambda</math>. Other factorisations of the potential <math>V</math> can be considered as well.<ref name="BtEG2022">{{cite journal | last1 = Behrndt | first1 = J. | last2 = ter Elst | first2 = A. F. M. | last3 = Gesztesy | first3 = F. | title = The generalized Birman–Schwinger principle | journal = Transactions of the American Mathematical Society | volume = 375 | pages = 799–845 | year = 2022 | issue = 2 | arxiv= 2005.01195 | doi= 10.1090/tran/8401}}</ref>

More generally, the principle can be established for operators of the form <math>A - B</math>. In both the self-adjoint<ref name="FLW2022"/> and non self-adjoint cases,<ref name="BtEG2022"/> the Birman–Schwinger principle connects eigenvalues <math>\lambda</math> of <math>A - B</math> to the eigenvalue 1 of <math>B_1 (A - \lambda)^{-1} B_2^*</math> for a suitable factorisation <math>B = B_2^* B_1</math>.
